Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger: the LORD shall swallow them up in his wrath, and the fire shall devour them."

question: What complete eradication of the wicked conspirators' lineage is prophesied in Psalm 21:10?
opt1: "Their silver shall be confiscated for the sanctuary, and their lands given unto the tribe of Levi;"
opt2: "Their names shall be blotted out of the tribal scrolls, and their bones scattered in the valley;"
opt3: "Their princes shall be chained in iron, and their daughters shall become handmaids in Zion;"
opt4: "Their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men."
correct: "Their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men."
explanation: Judicial cutting off of posterity: their offspring ('fruit') and descendants ('seed') are completely extinguished from human society. Psalm 21:10 (KJV) - "Their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth, and their seed from among the children of men."

question: Why did the enemies' schemes against the king utterly fail according to Psalm 21:11?
opt1: "For they intended evil against thee: they imagined a mischievous device, which they are not able to perform."
opt2: "Because their messengers were delayed by floods, and their archers lacked arrows;"
opt3: "Because the elders of Israel exposed their conspiracy, and their captains fled into the hills;"
opt4: "Because an angel of the Lord struck their camp at midnight, and destroyed their weapons;"
correct: "For they intended evil against thee: they imagined a mischievous device, which they are not able to perform."
explanation: Sinners plot elaborate evil against God's Anointed, but their malice is utterly impotent: they imagine mischievous schemes that they possess zero ability to execute. Psalm 21:11 (KJV) - "For they intended evil against thee: they imagined a mischievous device, which they are not able to perform."

question: What closing doxology of praise for divine omnipotence completes Psalm 21 in verse 13?
opt1: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting. Amen, and Amen;"
opt2: "Be thou exalted, LORD, in thine own strength: so will we sing and praise thy power."
opt3: "Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised in the city of our God;"
opt4: "Let everything that hath breath praise the Lord. Praise ye the Lord;"
correct: "Be thou exalted, LORD, in thine own strength: so will we sing and praise thy power."
explanation: The psalm concludes with a triumphant crescendo: exalting Yahweh in His own intrinsic power, with the redeemed community responding in perpetual song and praise. Psalm 21:13 (KJV) - "Be thou exalted, LORD, in thine own strength: so will we sing and praise thy power."

question: What historic cry of dereliction, uttered by Jesus Christ on the cross, opens Psalm 22:1?
opt1: "O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee: incline thine ear;"
opt2: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?"
opt3: "Hear my prayer, O God, give ear to my supplications: in thy faithfulness answer me;"
opt4: "Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul: I sink in deep mire;"
correct: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?"
explanation: Cited verbatim by Jesus in Aramaic ('Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani', Matt 27:46): the supreme prophetic portrait of the suffering Messiah enduring judicial abandonment for sinners. Psalm 22:1 (KJV) - "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?"

question: What theological truth regarding God's holiness and enthronement does the suffering Sufferer affirm in Psalm 22:3?
opt1: "For thou art righteous, dwelling in the secret pavilion of the tabernacle;"
opt2: "Yet thou art faithful, keeping the covenant made with the fathers of old;"
opt3: "But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel."
opt4: "Behold, thou art the King of glory, seated above the cherubim of Zion;"
correct: "But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel."
explanation: Even in the agony of forsakenness, the Sufferer refuses to charge God with injustice, reverently affirming that God is holy and enthroned upon Israel's praises. Psalm 22:3 (KJV) - "But thou art holy, O thou that inhabitest the praises of Israel."

question: With what humble self-description does the Sufferer contrast himself with the delivered patriarchs in Psalm 22:6?
opt1: "For I am as water poured out upon the earth, which cannot be gathered again;"
opt2: "Yet am I like a broken vessel, cast out of the sight of the living;"
opt3: "Behold, I am a fugitive and a vagabond, having no city of refuge;"
opt4: "But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people."
correct: "But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people."
explanation: While ancestral fathers trusted and were delivered, the Messiah was stripped of human dignity, crushed like a helpless scarlet worm (tola'at), mocked and despised by the public. Psalm 22:6 (KJV) - "But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised of the people."

question: What exact mocking gestures and words of the crucifiers are prophesied in Psalm 22:7-8?
opt1: Shooting out the lip, shaking the head, saying: "He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him."
opt2: Clapping their hands, hissing with their tongues, saying: "Behold the king without a crown;"
opt3: Casting stones, spitting upon his garments, saying: "Where is the God of Abraham to rescue thee;"
opt4: Bowing the knee in mockery, placing a reed in his hand, saying: "Prophesy who smote thee;"
correct: Shooting out the lip, shaking the head, saying: "He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him."
explanation: Fulfilled with chilling precision at Calvary (Matt 27:39, 43): the onlookers sneered, wagged their heads, and taunted Christ's trust in God using these identical words. Psalm 22:7-8 (KJV) - "All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying, He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him."

question: What anatomical description of crucifixion agony is detailed in Psalm 22:14-15?
opt1: Limb broken by iron rods, skin burned with fiery coals, eyes blinded by dust, marrow drained from bones
opt2: Poured out like water, bones out of joint, heart melted like wax in bowels, strength dried like a potsherd, tongue cleaving to jaws
opt3: Flesh torn by predatory beasts, veins emptied of blood, breath failing like a dying candle
opt4: Forehead pierced with thorns, shoulders bruised by the heavy wood, knees trembling through fasting
correct: Poured out like water, bones out of joint, heart melted like wax in bowels, strength dried like a potsherd, tongue cleaving to jaws
explanation: Clinical foretelling of crucifixion: extreme dehydration, dislocated joints under hanging weight, cardiac failure ('heart melted like wax'), and parched tongue ('I thirst'). Psalm 22:14-15 (KJV) - "I am poured out like water, and all my bones are out of joint: my heart is like wax; it is melted in the midst of my bowels. My strength is dried up like a potsherd; and my tongue cleaveth to my jaws; and thou hast brought me into the dust of death."

question: What astonishing explicit prophecy of the crucifixion wounds appears in Psalm 22:16?
opt1: "For the archers have wounded me: they have shot their arrows into my side and my thighs;"
opt2: "For the executioners have bound me: they have scourged my back with thirty-nine stripes;"
opt3: "For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet."
opt4: "For false witnesses have condemned me: they have cast me down from the rock of Zion;"
correct: "For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet."
explanation: Written a thousand years before Roman crucifixion was invented: Gentile mobs ('dogs') surround the Messiah and pierce His hands and feet with nails. Psalm 22:16 (KJV) - "For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet."

question: What division of personal property by lot is foretold in Psalm 22:18?
opt1: "They divide my silver among the soldiers, and sell my sandals for bread;"
opt2: "They tear my seamless tunic in pieces, and cast lots for my royal signet ring;"
opt3: "They burn my books of prayer, and give my linen mantle unto the high priest;"
opt4: "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture."
correct: "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture."
explanation: Fulfilled literally at the foot of the cross when Roman soldiers divided Jesus' outer garments into four parts and gambled for His seamless tunic (John 19:23-24). Psalm 22:18 (KJV) - "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture."

question: What dramatic transition from suffering to global proclamation occurs in Psalm 22:22?
opt1: "I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee."
opt2: "I will return from the grave in power: and destroy the Roman cohorts with fire;"
opt3: "I will ascend into the heavens with shouting: and take my seat upon the throne of David;"
opt4: "I will summon the twelve tribes of Israel: and rebuild the temple upon Mount Moriah;"
correct: "I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee."
explanation: Quoted in Hebrews 2:12: the risen Messiah declares the Father's name to His redeemed disciples ('brethren') and leads the corporate praise of the Church. Psalm 22:22 (KJV) - "I will declare thy name unto my brethren: in the midst of the congregation will I praise thee."

question: What global Gentile conversion and kingdom dominion are prophesied in Psalm 22:27-28?
opt1: "All the kings of the earth shall bring gold from Ophir: and the princes of Tyre shall bow before Zion;"
opt2: "All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD: and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee. For the kingdom is the LORD'S: and he is the governor among the nations."
opt3: "The nations shall beat their swords into plowshares: and study war no more forever;"
opt4: "The heathen shall become woodcutters in the sanctuary: and serve the sons of Aaron in the temple;"
correct: "All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD: and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee. For the kingdom is the LORD'S: and he is the governor among the nations."
explanation: The fruit of Christ's cross: worldwide evangelization where all ethnic families ('kindreds of the nations') turn in worship to Yahweh, the sovereign Governor of nations. Psalm 22:27-28 (KJV) - "All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD: and all the kindreds of the nations shall worship before thee. For the kingdom is the LORD'S: and he is the governor among the nations."

question: What final triumphant declaration of completed righteousness concludes Psalm 22:31, echoing 'It is finished'?
opt1: "The seed of Jacob shall reign from sea to sea, and no adversary shall arise;"
opt2: "The glory of the Lord shall fill the earth as the waters cover the sea;"
opt3: "They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this."
opt4: "Blessed be the name of the Lord from generation to generation forever;"
correct: "They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this."
explanation: The Hebrew closing phrase 'asah' ('he hath done this') corresponds to the dying cry on the cross 'Tetelestai' ('It is finished' - John 19:30), declaring the work of redemption fully accomplished. Psalm 22:31 (KJV) - "They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this."

question: What foundational confession of divine pastoral care and total contentment opens Psalm 23:1?
opt1: "The Lord is my light and my fortress; whom shall I fear?"
opt2: "The Lord is my rock and my fortress; I will not be moved;"
opt3: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want."
opt4: "The Lord is my shield and my reward; I will dwell in peace;"
correct: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want."
explanation: Invoking God as Yahweh-Rohi (The LORD My Shepherd), David confesses total satisfaction and absence of lack under the Good Shepherd's care. Psalm 23:1 (KJV) - "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want."

question: Where does the Good Shepherd provide restful nourishment and peaceful refreshment in Psalm 23:2?
opt1: Leads him into fortified sheepfolds, and feeds him with the finest of wheat
opt2: Guides him to the high mountain terraces, and gives him fresh wine from the vats
opt3: Brings him into the royal palace, and pours out sweet honey from the rock
opt4: Makes him to lie down in green pastures, and leads him beside the still waters
correct: Makes him to lie down in green pastures, and leads him beside the still waters
explanation: The Shepherd satisfies both physical and spiritual thirst: lush budding meadows ('green pastures') for rest, and waters of quietness ('still waters') for refreshment. Psalm 23:2 (KJV) - "He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters."

question: What spiritual revival and moral guidance does the Shepherd provide in Psalm 23:3?
opt1: "He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake."
opt2: "He healeth my diseases: He guideth my feet over the desert for the fathers' sake;"
opt3: "He forgiveth my iniquity: He directeth my steps toward Zion for His mercy's sake;"
opt4: "He reneweth my youth: He establisheth my goings in safety for the covenant's sake;"
correct: "He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake."
explanation: When the sheep strays or grows weary, God restores the soul (repentance/renewal) and steers the believer on well-worn righteous paths for the honor of His own Name. Psalm 23:3 (KJV) - "He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake."

question: What fearless confidence does the believer express when walking through death's gloom in Psalm 23:4?
opt1: "Even if the armies of darkness encamp around me, I will not tremble: for thine angels shield my head;"
opt2: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."
opt3: "Though my bones sink into the grave, I shall not be moved: for thy right hand will raise me up;"
opt4: "Though the tempest of the wilderness rage, I shall abide in safety: for the rock covers me;"
correct: "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."
explanation: Notice the grammatical shift from talking *about* God ('He') to talking *to* God ('Thou art with me'): divine personal presence dispels all dread in deep, dark ravines. Psalm 23:4 (KJV) - "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."

question: What distinct pastoral functions do the 'rod' and 'staff' serve in comforting the sheep in Psalm 23:4?
opt1: The rod measures the wool during shearing, while the staff marks the boundary of pasture
opt2: The rod is used to discipline stubborn sheep, while the staff is used to dig for mountain springs
opt3: The rod defends against attacking predators, while the crook-headed staff guides, directs, and rescues entangled sheep
opt4: The rod counts the flock at sunset, while the staff is used to signal the assistant shepherds
correct: The rod defends against attacking predators, while the crook-headed staff guides, directs, and rescues entangled sheep
explanation: The short oak club ('rod') was a weapon of defense against wolves and lions, while the longer crook ('staff') was an instrument of tender guidance and rescue. Psalm 23:4 (KJV) - "Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me."

question: What transition from Shepherd to Royal Host occurs in Psalm 23:5, and what hospitality is bestowed?
opt1: Pours out the blood of the sacrifices, washes the feet with rosewater, and clothes in purple robes
opt2: Places a golden crown upon the head, gives the scepter of Judah, and serves bread of angels
opt3: Builds a pavilion of cedar, gives the key of David, and fills the storehouses with grain
opt4: Prepares a table in the presence of enemies, anoints the head with oil, and causes the cup to run over
correct: Prepares a table in the presence of enemies, anoints the head with oil, and causes the cup to run over
explanation: God acts as a lavish, hospitable Host: spreading a banquet under the very gaze of frustrated enemies, anointing the guest with refreshing perfumed oil, and overflowing his cup. Psalm 23:5 (KJV) - "Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over."

question: What two divine guardian companions pursue the believer throughout earthly life in Psalm 23:6?
opt1: Goodness and mercy: "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life ..."
opt2: Grace and truth: "Verily grace and truth shall encompass my steps in all my ways ..."
opt3: Light and salvation: "Truly light and salvation shall go before my face forever ..."
opt4: Peace and righteousness: "Righteousness and peace shall kiss each other before my tent ..."
correct: Goodness and mercy: "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life ..."
explanation: Hebrew 'radaph' (normally used of enemies chasing down victims) is here inverted: God's covenant goodness (tov) and unfailing mercy (hesed) actively hunt down and accompany the believer daily. Psalm 23:6 (KJV) - "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever."

question: With what eternal destination and residency does Psalm 23 conclude in verse 6?
opt1: "And I will sing praises upon Mount Zion unto endless ages."
opt2: "And I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever."
opt3: "And I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living."
opt4: "And my soul shall rest under the shadow of the Almighty world without end."
correct: "And I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever."
explanation: The ultimate climax: the believer is not merely an occasional visitor, but a permanent family member dwelling in Yahweh's presence for the length of unending days. Psalm 23:6 (KJV) - "Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever."

question: What is the meaning of the phrase 'my cup runneth over' in Psalm 23:5?
opt1: Accidental spillage of wine during an awkward formal royal ceremony
opt2: A sacrificial libation poured out on the ground as an offering to God
opt3: Superabundant, overflowing divine provision and joy that exceeds all capacity to contain it
opt4: An empty vessel waiting to be filled with the waters of the river Jordan
correct: Superabundant, overflowing divine provision and joy that exceeds all capacity to contain it
explanation: In Near Eastern hospitality, a cup filled to the brim showed generous welcome, but a cup filled until it ran over demonstrated ecstatic, boundless royal lavishness. Psalm 23:5 (KJV) - "Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over."

question: Why does the psalmist say God leads him in paths of righteousness 'for his name's sake' in Psalm 23:3?
opt1: Because David had paid five hundred shekels of silver into the sanctuary fund
opt2: Because the Levitical priests required a public proclamation of the divine name
opt3: Because an oath sworn by the high priest had to be repeated every seventh year
opt4: Because God's own covenant reputation and moral character are pledged to guide and preserve His people faithfully
correct: Because God's own covenant reputation and moral character are pledged to guide and preserve His people faithfully
explanation: A shepherd's reputation depends on the health and safe arrival of his sheep; God guides us rightly because His own holy name and glory are at stake. Psalm 23:3 (KJV) - "He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake."

question: What universal declaration of God's absolute ownership of the cosmos opens Psalm 24:1-2?
opt1: "The heavens belong unto the Lord, and the stars thereof; the dry land He hath given unto the children of Adam;"
opt2: "Zion is the habitation of the Almighty, and the sanctuary thereof; the heathen are His footstool;"
opt3: "The kingdom is the Lord's, and the glory thereof; all kings of the earth shall bow down before Him;"
opt4: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. For he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods."
correct: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. For he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods."
explanation: Cited by Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:26: Yahweh is the exclusive Creator and Owner of the entire earth, its resources, its geography, and all human inhabitants. Psalm 24:1-2 (KJV) - "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. For he hath founded it upon the seas, and established it upon the floods."

question: What two searching questions regarding entrance into God's presence are asked in Psalm 24:3?
opt1: "Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?"
opt2: "Who can abide the day of His coming? and who shall stand when He appeareth?"
opt3: "Who is like unto thee, O Lord, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness?"
opt4: "Who shall bring a clean thing out of an unclean? who can fathom the mind of the Almighty?"
correct: "Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?"
explanation: An entrance liturgy originally sung when the Ark of the Covenant was brought up Mount Zion: who is spiritually worthy to approach God's sanctuary? Psalm 24:3 (KJV) - "Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?"

question: What four moral and spiritual qualifications define the acceptable worshiper in Psalm 24:4?
opt1: Royal lineage, vast offerings of silver, observance of new moons, and military victories
opt2: Clean hands, a pure heart, not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully
opt3: Wearing white linen, fasting forty days, memorizing the Torah, and offering bullocks
opt4: Circumcised on the eighth day, free from bodily blemishes, of the tribe of Levi, and zealous for the law
correct: Clean hands, a pure heart, not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully
explanation: True access to God requires outward integrity of actions ('clean hands'), inward purity of desires ('pure heart'), refusal of idolatry ('not lifted soul to vanity'), and honesty in oaths. Psalm 24:4 (KJV) - "He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully."

question: What two divine gifts will the authentic worshiper receive from God according to Psalm 24:5?
opt1: "He shall receive length of days from the Lord, and an inheritance of land in the valley of Eshcol;"
opt2: "He shall receive a crown of pure gold, and victory over all the Philistine cities;"
opt3: "He shall receive the blessing from the LORD, and righteousness from the God of his salvation."
opt4: "He shall receive the oil of gladness, and his children shall be multiplied like the stars;"
correct: "He shall receive the blessing from the LORD, and righteousness from the God of his salvation."
explanation: Those who seek God receive divine benediction ('blessing') and imputed, practical vindication ('righteousness') from the God who saves them. Psalm 24:5 (KJV) - "He shall receive the blessing from the LORD, and righteousness from the God of his salvation."

question: How is the community of true worshipers defined in Psalm 24:6?
opt1: "This is the assembly of the priests of Aaron, that minister at the golden altar of incense;"
opt2: "This is the host of David's mighty men, that have broken the gates of the Jebusites;"
opt3: "This is the remnant of the twelve tribes, that keep the Passover in the first month;"
opt4: "This is the generation of them that seek him, that seek thy face, O Jacob. Selah."
correct: "This is the generation of them that seek him, that seek thy face, O Jacob. Selah."
explanation: The true Israel of God: not mere physical descent, but a generation characterized by earnest, single-minded pursuit of God's face like wrestling Jacob (Gen 32:30). Psalm 24:6 (KJV) - "This is the generation of them that seek him, that seek thy face, O Jacob. Selah."

question: What majestic command is addressed to the ancient city gates in Psalm 24:7?
opt1: "Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in."
opt2: "Open wide your portals, O ye towers of Zion; let the archers of Judah enter with shouting;"
opt3: "Unbar the iron gates, O daughter of Jerusalem; make way for the chariot of the king;"
opt4: "Rend your battlements, O ancient walls; bow down before the ark of the covenant of the Lord;"
correct: "Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in."
explanation: Personifying the ancient city gates of Jerusalem (and symbolically the celestial gates of heaven), the herald commands them to expand upward to welcome the glorious King. Psalm 24:7 (KJV) - "Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in."

question: What question and answer regarding the King's identity are exchanged in Psalm 24:8?
opt1: "Who is this King of glory? David the son of Jesse, the ruler over the tribes of Israel;"
opt2: "Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle."
opt3: "Who is this King of glory? The angel of the covenant, who divided the waters of the Red Sea;"
opt4: "Who is this King of glory? The high priest of the sanctuary, clothed in holy garments;"
correct: "Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle."
explanation: The watchmen at the gate challenge the approaching procession; the chorus responds that the King is Yahweh Himself, invincible in military combat and triumphant over all foes. Psalm 24:8 (KJV) - "Who is this King of glory? The LORD strong and mighty, the LORD mighty in battle."

question: What repeated anthem and climactic revelation of God's supreme title concludes Psalm 24 in verses 9-10?
opt1: "Open the doors of the temple ... Who is this King of glory? The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Amen;"
opt2: "Bow down ye nations ... Who is this King of glory? The Holy One of Israel, the Creator of the ends of the earth;"
opt3: "Lift up your heads, O ye gates ... Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory. Selah."
opt4: "Shout aloud ye tribes ... Who is this King of glory? The Prince of Peace, whose kingdom shall have no end;"
correct: "Lift up your heads, O ye gates ... Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory. Selah."
explanation: The solemn challenge is repeated, culminating in the supreme military-covenantal title 'Yahweh Sabaoth' (The LORD of Hosts / Commander of angelic armies), who is the King of Glory. Psalm 24:9-10 (KJV) - "Lift up your heads, O ye gates; even lift them up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in. Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory. Selah."

question: What historical occasion in 2 Samuel 6 likely served as the original context for the composition of Psalm 24?
opt1: Solomon dedicating the first temple upon Mount Moriah
opt2: Joshua carrying the ark across the flooded river Jordan
opt3: Hezekiah celebrating the great Passover after cleansing the temple
opt4: David bringing the Ark of the Covenant up from the house of Obed-edom into the newly captured city of Jerusalem
correct: David bringing the Ark of the Covenant up from the house of Obed-edom into the newly captured city of Jerusalem
explanation: Psalm 24 was composed for the grand procession when David transported the Ark (the earthly throne of Yahweh) into the Jebusite citadel of Zion, making Jerusalem the City of God. Psalm 24:7 (KJV) - "Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in."

question: How do Psalms 22, 23, and 24 form a famous Christological Shepherd Trilogy in biblical theology?
opt1: Psalm 22 presents the Good Shepherd dying for the sheep (past); Psalm 23 presents the Great Shepherd caring for the sheep (present); Psalm 24 presents the Chief Shepherd reigning in glory (future)
opt2: Psalm 22 depicts the Shepherd in Bethlehem; Psalm 23 in Galilee; Psalm 24 in Nazareth
opt3: Psalm 22 shows the Shepherd fighting Goliath; Psalm 23 fleeing Saul; Psalm 24 ruling in Hebron
opt4: Psalm 22 reveals the Shepherd of Israel; Psalm 23 the Shepherd of Judah; Psalm 24 the Shepherd of Levi
correct: Psalm 22 presents the Good Shepherd dying for the sheep (past); Psalm 23 presents the Great Shepherd caring for the sheep (present); Psalm 24 presents the Chief Shepherd reigning in glory (future)
explanation: The Shepherd Trilogy reveals the Good Shepherd giving His life in death, the Great Shepherd guiding in life, and the Chief Shepherd entering Zion in glory. Psalm 24:7 (KJV) - "Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in."

question: With what upward posture of surrender and trust does David open Psalm 25:1-2?
opt1: "Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul. O my God, I trust in thee: let me not be ashamed, let not mine enemies triumph over me."
opt2: "Unto thee, O Lord, do I pour out my complaint: in thee is my refuge, let not the wicked take my life;"
opt3: "Unto the sanctuary do I direct my eyes, O God of Israel: let not my feet slip upon the dark mountains;"
opt4: "Unto thy throne do I lift up my hands in prayer: let not the heathen mock my faith in the covenant;"
correct: "Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul. O my God, I trust in thee: let me not be ashamed, let not mine enemies triumph over me."
explanation: David opens this acrostic psalm offering his entire inner being ('lift up my soul') to Yahweh, praying that his faith will never be humiliated by enemy triumph. Psalm 25:1-2 (KJV) - "Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul. O my God, I trust in thee: let me not be ashamed, let not mine enemies triumph over me."

question: What fourfold guidance in divine truth does David plead for in Psalm 25:4-5?
opt1: "Write thy law upon my heart; guide my feet by thy light; instruct my mind in thy decrees; make my path straight;"
opt2: "Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths. Lead me in thy truth, and teach me: for thou art the God of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day."
opt3: "Send thine angel before my face; teach me the proverbs of the wise; open mine ears to reproof; hold my hand;"
opt4: "Reveal thy mysteries unto my soul; teach me the songs of Zion; lead me beside still waters; defend my goings;"
correct: "Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths. Lead me in thy truth, and teach me: for thou art the God of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day."
explanation: David seeks comprehensive discipleship: showing divine ways, teaching divine paths, leading in divine truth, and persevering in daily expectant waiting. Psalm 25:4-5 (KJV) - "Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths. Lead me in thy truth, and teach me: for thou art the God of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day."

question: What contrast between God's eternal mercies and David's past transgressions is drawn in Psalm 25:6-7?
opt1: Remember the sacrifices of the fathers, but forget the murmurings of the wilderness generation
opt2: Remember the covenant with Abraham, but blot out the failings of the kings of Judah
opt3: Remember tender mercies and lovingkindnesses of old, but remember not the sins of his youth nor his transgressions
opt4: Remember the blood of the Passover lamb, but judge not the secret thoughts of the heart
correct: Remember tender mercies and lovingkindnesses of old, but remember not the sins of his youth nor his transgressions
explanation: David asks God to recall His eternal, ancient mercies (hesed), while completely forgetting and wiping away the foolish sins and rebellions of his youth. Psalm 25:6-7 (KJV) - "Remember, O LORD, thy tender mercies and thy lovingkindnesses; for they have been ever of old. Remember not the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions: according to thy mercy remember thou me for thy goodness' sake, O LORD."

question: Whom will the good and upright LORD guide in judgment and instruct in His way according to Psalm 25:8-9?
opt1: He will teach the priests in the sanctuary, and the mighty will He guide in battle
opt2: He will instruct the princes of Judah, and the wealthy will He guide into prosperity
opt3: He will teach the elders of the gate, and the swift will He guide over the mountains
opt4: He will teach sinners in the way, and the meek will He guide in judgment and teach His way
correct: He will teach sinners in the way, and the meek will He guide in judgment and teach His way
explanation: Because God is inherently good, He lovingly instructs repentant sinners; and because the humble ('meek') are teachable, He guides them in justice. Psalm 25:8-9 (KJV) - "Good and upright is the LORD: therefore will he teach sinners in the way. The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way."

question: What are all the paths of the LORD declared to be for covenant-keepers in Psalm 25:10?
opt1: "All the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth unto such as keep his covenant and his testimonies."
opt2: "All the ways of the Lord are peace and prosperity unto them that bring tithes to the temple;"
opt3: "All the statutes of the Almighty are light and salvation unto the children of Abraham;"
opt4: "All the decrees of God are holiness and glory unto those that sacrifice bullocks;"
correct: "All the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth unto such as keep his covenant and his testimonies."
explanation: Every single path of God's providence—even painful trials—is saturated with covenant love ('mercy') and fidelity ('truth') for those obedient to His Word. Psalm 25:10 (KJV) - "All the paths of the LORD are mercy and truth unto such as keep his covenant and his testimonies."

question: What paradoxical reason does David give when pleading for the pardon of his iniquity in Psalm 25:11?
opt1: "For my youth's sake, O Lord, forgive my transgression; for it was unintentional;"
opt2: "For thy name's sake, O LORD, pardon mine iniquity; for it is great."
opt3: "For the temple's sake, O God, blot out my sin; for I have offered seven ram lambs;"
opt4: "For David's sake, O Almighty, remit my debt; for my enemies are fierce;"
correct: "For thy name's sake, O LORD, pardon mine iniquity; for it is great."
explanation: A magnificent gospel prayer: David does not minimize his sin, but confesses that his iniquity is enormous ('for it is great'), appealing solely to the glory of God's Name for pardon. Psalm 25:11 (KJV) - "For thy name's sake, O LORD, pardon mine iniquity; for it is great."

question: What intimate friendship and revelation does God share with those who revere Him in Psalm 25:14?
opt1: "The wealth of the Lord is with them that serve him; and he will give them the gold of Ophir;"
opt2: "The glory of the Lord resteth on them that pray; and he will show them visions of angels;"
opt3: "The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant."
opt4: "The counsel of the Almighty is with the elders; and he will establish their dynasty forever;"
correct: "The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant."
explanation: Hebrew 'sod' signifies confidential, intimate counsel: God shares His secret communion and unveils the deep riches of His covenant to those who walk in reverent fear. Psalm 25:14 (KJV) - "The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him; and he will shew them his covenant."

question: Why are David's eyes perpetually directed toward the LORD in Psalm 25:15?
opt1: "Because my eyes fail with looking for the morning dawn across the hills of Judah;"
opt2: "Because the beauty of the sanctuary draweth my heart from the vanities of earth;"
opt3: "Because I wait for the sign of the prophet to march against the Philistine host;"
opt4: "Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net."
correct: "Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net."
explanation: Instead of staring in panic at the hunter's snare around his feet, David gazes upward into God's face, trusting Yahweh to untangle and release him from the trap. Psalm 25:15 (KJV) - "Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net."

question: What twin moral virtues does David ask to guard and preserve him in Psalm 25:21?
opt1: "Let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee."
opt2: "Let mercy and truth compass me; for I delight in thy holy law;"
opt3: "Let wisdom and knowledge be my shield; for I meditate upon thy statutes;"
opt4: "Let strength and honor be my clothing; for I dwell under the shadow of thy wings;"
correct: "Let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee."
explanation: David relies on personal integrity and ethical uprightness as moral bodyguards, keeping his character blameless as he patiently waits for God's vindication. Psalm 25:21 (KJV) - "Let integrity and uprightness preserve me; for I wait on thee."

question: What is the structural poetic design of Psalm 25 in the Hebrew text?
opt1: A royal wedding liturgy written in rhyming Aramaic couplets

opt4: A chiasm centered entirely upon the seven historical feasts of Israel
correct: An acrostic poem where successive verses begin with the consecutive letters of the Hebrew alphabet
explanation: Psalm 25 is an alphabetic acrostic (along with Psalms 9-10, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119, 145), facilitating memorization and symbolizing comprehensive devotional prayer. Psalm 25:1-22 (KJV) - "Unto thee, O LORD, do I lift up my soul ..."

question: What bold appeal to judicial examination and moral integrity opens Psalm 26:1-2?
opt1: "Hear me, O Lord, according to thy mercy: forgive my secret sins, lest I fall into the snare. Cleanse my lips, O God;"
opt2: "Judge me, O LORD; for I have walked in mine integrity: I have trusted also in the LORD; therefore I shall not slide. Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart."
opt3: "Plead my cause, O King of righteousness: avenge me of the Philistines, for my strength faileth. Search my thoughts;"
opt4: "Deliver me, O Shepherd of Israel: guide my steps beside the streams, lest I wander. Look upon my affliction;"
correct: "Judge me, O LORD; for I have walked in mine integrity: I have trusted also in the LORD; therefore I shall not slide. Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart."
explanation: David invites divine judicial scrutiny: confident of his blameless walk and unwavering faith in Yahweh, he asks God to smelt and assay his inner thoughts (heart) and motives (reins). Psalm 26:1-2 (KJV) - "Judge me, O LORD; for I have walked in mine integrity: I have trusted also in the LORD; therefore I shall not slide. Examine me, O LORD, and prove me; try my reins and my heart."

question: What constant vision motivates David's obedience and walk in Psalm 26:3?
opt1: "For the fear of thy wrath is in my heart: and I have kept the commandments of Moses;"
opt2: "For the beauty of Zion is in my memory: and I have offered the daily morning sacrifice;"
opt3: "For thy lovingkindness is before mine eyes: and I have walked in thy truth."
opt4: "For the crown of David is upon my brow: and I have executed justice in the gate;"
correct: "For thy lovingkindness is before mine eyes: and I have walked in thy truth."
explanation: David's holy living is not motivated by legalistic terror, but by constantly meditating upon God's lovingkindness (hesed), which inspires faithful adherence to truth. Psalm 26:3 (KJV) - "For thy lovingkindness is before mine eyes: and I have walked in thy truth."

question: What two types of deceptive individuals does David refuse to associate with in Psalm 26:4?
opt1: Foreign merchants, and uncircumcised Philistines
opt2: Corrupt tax collectors, and rebellious captains of Saul
opt3: False prophets of Baal, and astrologers of Babylon
opt4: Vain persons, and dissemblers (hypocrites)
correct: Vain persons, and dissemblers (hypocrites)
explanation: David maintains strict holy separation from empty, deceitful people ('vain persons') and two-faced hypocrites who conceal their real motives ('dissemblers'). Psalm 26:4 (KJV) - "I have not sat with vain persons, neither will I go in with dissemblers."

question: What corporate assembly does David vigorously detest in Psalm 26:5?
opt1: "I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked."
opt2: "I have rejected the council of the elders of Samaria; and will not enter their cities;"
opt3: "I have abhorred the feasts of the Ammonites; and will not drink their wine;"
opt4: "I have despised the assembly of the princes of Tyre; and will not accept their gifts;"
correct: "I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked."
explanation: David expresses holy antipathy toward organized wickedness, refusing to participate in the meetings, conspiracies, or gatherings of evil-doers. Psalm 26:5 (KJV) - "I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked."

question: What symbolic Levitical ritual does David perform before encircling God's altar in Psalm 26:6?
opt1: "I will anoint my head with oil: so will I blow the silver shofar before the ark;"
opt2: "I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar, O LORD:"
opt3: "I will put off my shoes from my feet: so will I bring the grain offering to the priests;"
opt4: "I will clothe myself in sackcloth: so will I sprinkle the blood of the bullock;"
correct: "I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar, O LORD:"
explanation: Echoing priestly washings at the bronze laver, David washes his hands in genuine moral purity ('innocency') before joining the joyful procession around God's altar. Psalm 26:6 (KJV) - "I will wash mine hands in innocency: so will I compass thine altar, O LORD:"

question: What two acts of public testimony does David intend to proclaim around the altar in Psalm 26:7?
opt1: Sing the victory of Moses at the Red Sea, and recount the boundaries of the tribes
opt2: Pronounce the seven blessings of Deuteronomy, and read the law before the assembly
opt3: Publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all God's wondrous works
opt4: Declare the lineage of the house of Jesse, and display the sword of Goliath of Gath
correct: Publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all God's wondrous works
explanation: Worship culminates in evangelistic proclamation: shouting vocal thanksgiving and enthusiastically narrating all of God's miraculous deeds to the congregation. Psalm 26:7 (KJV) - "That I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works."

question: What passionate love for the sanctuary does David express in Psalm 26:8?
opt1: "O God, I have built the cedar palace, and desired to make an ark of gold for thy name;"
opt2: "Lord, I have desired the courts of Zion above all the ivory palaces of the kings;"
opt3: "Almighty, I have preferred the gates of Jerusalem above all the tents of wickedness;"
opt4: "LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth."
correct: "LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth."
explanation: David's supreme delight is the sanctuary tabernacle, which he treasures as the earthly residence of God's manifest glory ('where thine honour dwelleth'). Psalm 26:8 (KJV) - "LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth."

question: What dreadful association and judicial grouping does David plead to avoid in Psalm 26:9-10?
opt1: Gather not his soul with sinners nor his life with bloody men, whose hands hold mischief and right hand is full of bribes

opt3: Count not his days among the false prophets nor his inheritance with the sons of Belial
opt4: Deliver not his body unto the plague nor his children into the chains of Babylon
correct: Gather not his soul with sinners nor his life with bloody men, whose hands hold mischief and right hand is full of bribes
explanation: Having separated himself from the wicked in life, David begs that God will not sweep his soul into common destruction with violent murderers and corrupt bribe-takers in judgment. Psalm 26:9-10 (KJV) - "Gather not my soul with sinners, nor my life with bloody men: In whose hands is mischief, and their right hand is full of bribes."

question: With what two declarations of sure footing and public praise does Psalm 26 conclude in verse 12?
opt1: "My feet are like hinds' feet: upon the high mountains will I shout for joy;"

opt3: "My steps are established upon the rock: before the elders will I sing praises;"
opt4: "My path is illuminated by the morning sun: in the gates of Zion will I rejoice;"
correct: "My foot standeth in an even place: in the congregations will I bless the LORD."
explanation: Instead of sliding (v. 1), David now stands securely on level, unshakeable ground ('an even place'), ready to bless Yahweh in the assembled congregation. Psalm 26:12 (KJV) - "My foot standeth in an even place: in the congregations will I bless the LORD."

question: What is the meaning of the archaic English word 'dissemblers' in Psalm 26:4?
opt1: Rioters who dismantle public stone monuments and altars
opt2: Cowardly soldiers who disband from military formation in battle
opt3: Hypocrites who conceal their real character, thoughts, or malicious designs behind a false exterior
opt4: Corrupt judges who dissolve valid legal contracts for money

explanation: 'Dissemblers' translates Hebrew 'na'alamim' (the hidden ones), denoting two-faced individuals who disguise their true motives to deceive others. Psalm 26:4 (KJV) - "I have not sat with vain persons, neither will I go in with dissemblers."

question: What triumphant double confession of fearless confidence opens Psalm 27:1?
opt1: "The Lord is my rock and my fortress; what can man do unto me? the Lord is my shield and my glory;"
opt2: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble; therefore will not we fear;"
opt3: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?"
opt4: "The Lord of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge; I will not be moved;"
correct: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?"
explanation: David banishes all terror with three divine titles: Yahweh is his illuminating Light (dispelling darkness), his Salvation (dispelling peril), and the Stronghold of his life. Psalm 27:1 (KJV) - "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?"

question: What happened when cannibalistic adversaries advanced to devour David's flesh in Psalm 27:2?
opt1: "The earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up with their swords and shields;"
opt2: "A fire went forth from the presence of the Lord, and consumed their mighty men;"
opt3: "An angel of the Lord smote their host with blindness, and they fled into the wilderness;"
opt4: "When the wicked, even mine enemies and my foes, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell."
correct: "When the wicked, even mine enemies and my foes, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell."
explanation: Though savage foes attacked like wild beasts to devour him alive, it was the attackers who inexplicably stumbled and collapsed in defeat. Psalm 27:2 (KJV) - "When the wicked, even mine enemies and my foes, came upon me to eat up my flesh, they stumbled and fell."

question: What singular, supreme lifelong ambition did David seek from the LORD in Psalm 27:4?
opt1: "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple."
opt2: "That I may conquer all the borders of the Philistines, and establish a dynasty of peace for my son Solomon;"
opt3: "That I may build a magnificent temple of cedar on Mount Moriah, adorned with gold of Ophir;"
opt4: "That my name may be remembered as the sweet psalmist of Israel, and my songs sung in every generation;"
correct: "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple."
explanation: David's 'unum necessarium' (one thing necessary): continuous fellowship in God's presence, beholding the delightful beauty (pleasantness) of Yahweh, and meditating in His temple. Psalm 27:4 (KJV) - "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple."

question: Where will God securely hide and elevate David during times of trouble in Psalm 27:5?
opt1: Hide him in the mountain caverns of En-gedi, and set him upon the royal throne of Hebron

opt3: Shield him with twelve legions of cherubim, and surround him with a wall of celestial fire

correct: Hide him in His pavilion, in the secret of His tabernacle, and set him high upon a rock
explanation: Three images of impregnable security: the royal pavilion tent, the inaccessible inner shrine of the tabernacle, and a towering basalt rock cliff far above enemy reach. Psalm 27:5 (KJV) - "For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me; he shall set me up upon a rock."

question: What spontaneous dialogue of divine command and heart response is recorded in Psalm 27:8?
opt1: "When thou saidst, Offer sacrifices at Zion; my soul said, Behold, I bring seven fat bullocks;"

opt3: "When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek."
opt4: "When thou saidst, Keep my commandments; my spirit replied, Thy law is sweeter than honey;"
correct: "When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek."
explanation: The heartbeat of true prayer: the moment God issues the invitation 'Seek My face', David's regenerated heart immediately echoes back: 'Thy face, LORD, will I seek!' Psalm 27:8 (KJV) - "When thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek."

question: What supreme assurance of divine adoption when closest earthly relationships fail is proclaimed in Psalm 27:10?
opt1: "Though my brethren desert me in the day of battle, the Lord will dispatch an army of angels;"
opt2: "Though my wife despise me from the window, God will honor my dancing before the ark;"
opt3: "Even if the kings of the earth unite against me, the Almighty will give me an everlasting kingdom;"
opt4: "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up."
correct: "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up."
explanation: Even if the deepest, most instinctive human bonds—parental love—should fail, Yahweh adopts, embraces, and fosters ('take me up') His child with unfailing loyalty. Psalm 27:10 (KJV) - "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up."

question: What path does David ask God to lead him in because of watchful adversaries in Psalm 27:11?
opt1: "Teach me thy way, O LORD, and lead me in a plain path, because of mine enemies."
opt2: "Direct my chariot into the valley, and make me victorious over the princes of the Philistines;"
opt3: "Hide my footsteps on the secret mountain trails, lest the hunters of Saul discover my camp;"
opt4: "Level the hills of opposition before my face, and scatter coals of fire upon the persecutors;"
correct: "Teach me thy way, O LORD, and lead me in a plain path, because of mine enemies."
explanation: Surrounded by malicious critics waiting for a misstep, David asks for a level, obstacle-free highway ('a plain path') of moral rectitude where he cannot stumble. Psalm 27:11 (KJV) - "Teach me thy way, O LORD, and lead me in a plain path, because of mine enemies."

question: What essential conviction prevented David from fainting in despair in Psalm 27:13?
opt1: "I had surrendered to the sword, unless I had remembered the promise spoken by the prophet Samuel;"
opt2: "I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living."
opt3: "I had perished in the cave, unless my mighty men had brought me water from the well of Bethlehem;"
opt4: "I had lost all hope, unless the high priest had shown me the breastplate of Urim and Thummim;"
correct: "I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living."
explanation: David would have completely collapsed under persecution had he not maintained absolute faith that he would experience God's tangible goodness here in this present earthly life ('in the land of the living'). Psalm 27:13 (KJV) - "I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living."

question: What ringing double exhortation of patient endurance concludes Psalm 27 in verse 14?
opt1: "Trust in the Lord with all thine heart: lean not unto thine own understanding: wait on the Lord;"
opt2: "Gird up your loins: quit you like men, be strong: the Lord of hosts will fight for you;"
opt3: "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD."
opt4: "Rejoice in the Lord always: and again I say, Rejoice: the peace of God shall keep your hearts;"
correct: "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD."
explanation: David counsels his own soul and all believers with a double command: patiently wait on Yahweh, stay courageous, and God will impart infused strength to the heart. Psalm 27:14 (KJV) - "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD."

question: What Hebrew word translated 'beauty' in Psalm 27:4 refers to the delightful pleasantness and graciousness of God?
opt1: 'Kavod' (heavy weight of external physical brightness)

opt3: 'Hadar' (regal majesty and monarchical pomp)
opt4: 'No'am' (sweetness, pleasantness, gracious loveliness)

explanation: The Hebrew 'no'am' describes God's delightful graciousness, sweet suitability, and moral loveliness that enraptures the soul in worship. Psalm 27:4 (KJV) - "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple."

question: What desperate consequence does David fear if his Rock remains silent to his prayer in Psalm 28:1?
opt1: "Lest I be swallowed up by the flood of ungodly men, and my name be forgotten in Israel;"
opt2: "Lest my enemies rejoice over my stumbling, and tear my kingdom into twelve pieces;"
opt3: "Lest I wander in the desert without water, and become prey unto the lions of the valley;"
opt4: "Unto thee will I cry, O LORD my rock; be not silent to me: lest, if thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit."
correct: "Unto thee will I cry, O LORD my rock; be not silent to me: lest, if thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit."
explanation: Divine silence is equated with death: if God refuses to answer, David will become like a decaying corpse descending into the dark abyss of Sheol/the pit. Psalm 28:1 (KJV) - "Unto thee will I cry, O LORD my rock; be not silent to me: lest, if thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit."

question: Toward what sacred architectural location does David lift up his hands in supplication in Psalm 28:2?

opt2: Toward the brazen altar of burnt offering in the outer court

opt4: Toward the mountain peaks of Mount Hermon in the north
correct: Toward His holy oracle (the Holy of Holies / Debir)
explanation: The 'holy oracle' (Hebrew 'debir') is the innermost sanctuary (Holy of Holies) where the Ark of the Covenant rested and God spoke between the cherubim. Psalm 28:2 (KJV) - "Hear the voice of my supplications, when I cry unto thee, when I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle."

question: What two-faced duplicity characterizes the workers of iniquity in Psalm 28:3?
opt1: They wear white garments in public, but sacrifice to idols in secret
opt2: They speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts
